questions.stem: The payment provider disputes a payout webhook: it says it never sent `evt_1`. Webhooks are signed with HMAC-SHA256 and a shared secret. Can the expense app prove to a third party that the provider sent it?

options.t: No: both sides hold the HMAC key, so the app could have made the tag itself
options.why: HMAC authenticates between the two key holders only. Proof to a third party needs a signature with the provider's private key.

options.t: Yes: a valid HMAC proves the provider's origin
options.why: It proves origin to you, because you did not send it. A judge cannot tell which key holder made it.

options.t: Yes, if the timestamp is inside the window
options.why: The timestamp stops replay. It says nothing about who computed the tag.

options.t: No, because SHA-256 hashes can be recomputed by anyone
options.why: That is true of a plain hash, not of HMAC: computing the tag needs the key.

questions.stem: A team signs webhooks as `SHA256(secret + body)` and checks that value. What can an attacker who sees one signed webhook do?

options.t: Append data to the body and compute a valid tag without the secret (length extension)
options.why: The SHA-256 output is its internal state; hashing can continue from it. HMAC's nested construction prevents this.

options.t: Nothing: the secret is mixed into the hash
options.why: Prefix-keyed Merkle–Damgård hashes are extendable. That is why HMAC exists.

options.t: Recover the secret from the hash
options.why: SHA-256 is not invertible. The attack forges tags without learning the secret.

options.t: Only replay the same webhook
options.why: Replay is possible without a timestamp check, but length extension is worse: new valid messages.

questions.stem: The receiver compares 32-byte tags with `==`, which returns at the first wrong byte, and the timing is measurable. In the worst case, about how many tries does a byte-by-byte forgery need?

options.why: 256 candidates per byte × 32 bytes. About half that on average.
That is guessing the whole tag at once. The timing leak lets the attacker fix one byte at a time.
That finds one byte. There are 32.
Same as guessing the whole tag. The leak turns a product into a sum.

questions.stem: A webhook with `t=1795300000` and a valid HMAC arrives at server time 1795300420. The tolerance is 300 s. Decision?

options.t: Reject: it is 420 s old, beyond the 300 s window; it may be a replay
options.why: 1795300420 − 1795300000 = 420 > 300. A valid tag on an old message is exactly what a replay looks like.

options.t: Accept: the HMAC is valid
options.why: The tag proves the provider made it once, not that this is the first delivery.

options.t: Accept, then check the tag again later
options.why: Re-checking the same tag adds nothing. The age check is the replay control.

options.t: Reject: the HMAC must be wrong because the time is off
options.why: The tag can be valid. The age alone is the reason.

questions.stem: The auth service signs access tokens with HS256 and the same secret is configured in six verifying services. One of them is compromised. Impact?

options.t: The attacker can mint valid tokens for any user and any service
options.why: With HMAC, verifying and signing use the same key. Use ES256 or EdDSA: verifiers hold only public keys.

options.t: The attacker can read token payloads
options.why: Payloads were never secret: JWTs are signed, not encrypted.

options.t: Only that one service is at risk
options.why: The shared secret is valid everywhere, so forged tokens work on all six.

options.t: Nothing, if tokens expire in 15 minutes
options.why: The attacker mints new tokens with any `exp` they like.

questions.stem: An audit finds two ECDSA signatures from the same key with the same `r` value but different messages. What does it mean?

options.t: The nonce $k$ was reused; the private key can be computed from the two signatures
options.why: $r$ comes from $kG$. With the same $k$: $k = (z_1 - z_2)/(s_1 - s_2)$, then $d = (s_1 k - z_1)/r$ mod $n$.

options.t: Nothing: `r` is public and may repeat
options.why: `r` repeats only if $k$ repeats (or by negligible chance). It is the fingerprint of nonce reuse.

options.t: The two messages had the same hash
options.why: Different messages with SHA-256 do not collide in practice; and $r$ does not depend on the message.

options.t: Only those two signatures can be forged
options.why: Worse: the private key leaks, so every future signature can be forged. Rotate the key.

questions.stem: A leaked table has unsalted SHA-256 hashes. Passwords are 8 characters, lowercase + digits. The attacker's GPU does $10^{10}$ SHA-256 guesses/s. Time to try every such password?

options.t: About 5 minutes
About 89 years
options.why: That is the rate of a slow hash ($10^3$/s), e.g. Argon2id.

options.t: About 6 hours
options.why: That is the space for upper + lower + digits: $62^8 / 10^{10} \approx 2.2 \times 10^4$ s. Here it is lowercase + digits, $36^8$.

options.t: Centuries, because SHA-256 has 256-bit output
options.why: The output size is irrelevant. The attacker searches the password space, not the hash space.

questions.stem: Same attacker and space, but 1 million users. How does a per-user salt change the cost of cracking **all** accounts with fast SHA-256?

options.t: From one 5-minute pass to one pass per user: about 9 years
options.why: Without salt one pass tests every hash at once. With salt each user needs a separate pass: $10^6 \times 282$ s ≈ 8.9 years.

options.t: No change: the salt is stored next to the hash
options.why: Knowing the salt is fine. It still forces a separate search per user.

options.t: It makes cracking impossible
options.why: Each single account still falls in about 5 minutes. Salt multiplies by users; slowness needs a password hash.

options.t: It slows every guess by the salt length
options.why: A salt adds no per-guess cost. Argon2id / scrypt / bcrypt / PBKDF2 do.

questions.stem: To encrypt an export with a user passphrase, the code derives the key as `HKDF-SHA256(passphrase, salt)`. What is wrong?

options.t: HKDF is fast and adds no entropy, so a weak passphrase can be guessed at hash speed; use a password KDF like Argon2id
options.why: RFC 5869 §4: HKDF concentrates entropy but cannot amplify it; it has no slow-down.

options.t: Nothing: the salt makes it safe
options.why: A salt stops tables, not fast guessing.

options.t: HKDF output is too short for AES-256
options.why: HKDF can output any length you ask for. The problem is guessing cost.

options.t: HKDF needs a secret pepper
options.why: A pepper adds defence in depth, but the derivation is still fast.

questions.stem: One AES-GCM key encrypts every receipt, with random 96-bit nonces, at 10,000 encryptions/s. When does it reach NIST's $2^{32}$ limit, and what is the collision chance there?

options.t: After about 5 days; about $2^{-33}$
After about 50 days; about $2^{-33}$
options.why: That is 1,000 encryptions/s.

options.t: Never: 96 bits allow $2^{96}$ messages
options.why: Random nonces collide by the birthday bound long before $2^{96}$.

options.t: After about 5 days; about 50%
options.why: 50% is near $q = 2^{48}$. At $2^{32}$ the chance is tiny; the limit keeps it so.

questions.stem: The payouts service moves to `pay.expenses.example`, but still serves the certificate issued for `api.expenses.example`. Clients fail. Why?

options.t: Hostname mismatch: the name the client connected to is not in the certificate's SAN list
options.why: Chain and dates can be fine; the client still rejects a certificate for a different name.

options.t: The chain is missing an intermediate
options.why: That breaks validation too, but the change here is the name.

options.t: The certificate expired
options.why: Nothing in the move changes the dates.

options.t: mTLS requires the client to present the same certificate
options.why: In mTLS the client presents its own certificate, not the server's.

questions.stem: Explain envelope encryption for the 10 TB of receipts: who holds which key, what is stored with each receipt, and what rotating or revoking the master key costs.
questions.answer: Each receipt is encrypted locally with its own data key (DEK) using AES-GCM. The KMS master key (KEK) never leaves the KMS; it wraps each DEK, and the wrapped DEK is stored next to the ciphertext. To read, the service sends the wrapped DEK to the KMS, gets the DEK back (a logged, access-controlled call) and decrypts. Rotating the KEK means at most re-wrapping the DEKs (50 million × ~200 bytes ≈ 10 GB instead of 10 TB), and KMS automatic rotation often keeps old versions so nothing is re-wrapped. Revoking means disabling the KEK or the permission: every receipt becomes unreadable at once without touching the data. A key per object also keeps each key far below the GCM nonce limit.

sd-08-patterns.title: Design patterns: SOLID, GoF and ports and adapters
sd-08-patterns.source: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns (1994); Martin, Agile Software Development (2002) and Clean Architecture (2017); Meyer, Object-Oriented Software Construction (1988); Liskov & Wing, A Behavioral Notion of Subtyping (1994); Cockburn, Hexagonal Architecture (2005); Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) and Refactoring (1999); Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003); Bloch, Effective Java (Builder); Python docs: dataclasses, typing.Protocol (PEP 544), abc, functools. Illustrative numbers
sd-08-patterns.intro:
Student notes. One example runs to the end: the **shipping service** of an online store.
It quotes a price, books a carrier, prints a label and tracks the parcel.
Three carriers today: **Postal**, **Courier**, **Freight**. Three parcel types: **Letter**, **Box**, **Pallet**.
Question of the note: where does each new requirement go, so that it touches one place? Code is Python.

objectives.text: the five SOLID principles and the test for each
look-alike patterns: Adapter, Facade and Decorator; Strategy and Template method; Observer and pub-sub; command and event
the cost of a change under each design: edit points, class counts, decorator stacking
a design smell, and name the principle or pattern that fixes it
dependency inversion, injection and hexagonal architecture, and why they make tests fast

sections.title: 1. SOLID: five tests
sections.body:
- **S, single responsibility**: a module has one reason to change (one group of people asking for changes).
  - Example: `ShipmentService` quotes prices, calls the carrier HTTP APIs, renders the PDF label and emails the customer.
  - Four reasons to change: pricing rules, carrier API, label layout, email text → split into four parts.
- **O, open/closed** (Meyer): open for extension, closed for modification.
  - Example: `if carrier == "postal": ... elif ...` repeated in `quote`, `book`, `track`, `cancel`.
  - Adding a 4th carrier edits **4** existing functions. With one class per carrier behind an interface: **0** edits, 1 new class + 1 registry line.
- **L, Liskov substitution**: a subtype must work wherever its base works, without surprising callers.
  - No stronger preconditions, no weaker guarantees, no new exceptions.
  - Example: `FreightCarrier.track()` raises `NotImplementedError` → a loop over all carriers crashes.
  - Fix: a separate `Trackable` interface, or a contract result such as "no tracking".
  - It is about behavior. Same signature + surprising behavior still breaks it.
- **I, interface segregation**: clients should not depend on methods they do not use. Split fat interfaces into role interfaces.
  - Example: the price page needs only `rate()`. Give it a read-only `RateSource`, not the full `CarrierService` with `book`, `cancel`, `refund`.
- **D, dependency inversion**: core logic depends on abstractions it owns; IO adapters implement them (section 2).

sections.title: 2. Dependency inversion, injection, singletons
sections.body:
- **Dependency inversion** = a principle about the direction of source dependencies.
  - Without it: `pricing.py` imports `requests` and the carrier SDK. Core → IO.
  - With it: `pricing.py` defines `RateSource`; `postal_http.py` implements it. IO → core.
- **Dependency injection** = a technique: pass dependencies in (constructor or argument).
  - Production passes the real HTTP adapter; tests pass a fake that returns fixed rates.
```python
class RateSource(Protocol):
    def rate(self, parcel: Parcel) -> Money: ...

class Quoter:
    def __init__(self, sources: list[RateSource]):
        self.sources = sources
    def cheapest(self, parcel: Parcel) -> Money:
        return min((s.rate(parcel) for s in self.sources), key=lambda m: m.cents)
```
- Interfaces in Python:
  - `typing.Protocol`: **structural**. Any class with the right methods fits; no inheritance. Adapters stay decoupled from your base classes.
  - `abc.ABC`: **nominal**. Must inherit (or be registered). Refuses to instantiate a subclass missing an abstract method.
  - `isinstance` on a Protocol needs `@runtime_checkable`, and checks only that the methods exist, not their signatures.
- **Singleton**: one instance + a global access point.
  - Problem: hidden global state. Tests share it, cannot swap it, and every caller is coupled to it.
  - One instance is fine. Global access is the problem.
  - Fix: create one `CarrierClient` at startup (the composition root) and inject it.
  - A module-level object imported everywhere is a singleton too, with the same problems.

sections.title: 3. Creating objects: Factory and Builder
sections.body:
- **Factory**: a function or class that chooses the concrete type, so callers do not depend on it.
  - Example: `carrier_for(code)` looks up `{"postal": PostalCarrier, ...}` and returns a `Carrier`.
  - New carrier = 1 class + 1 registry entry. Callers unchanged.
  - GoF names: **Factory Method** (a subclass decides what to create), **Abstract Factory** (a family of related objects). A plain factory function is the everyday Python form.
- **Builder**: construct a complex object step by step, then `build()`, which validates the whole.
  - Example: a shipment with 4 optional parts: insurance, signature, customs form, delivery window → $2^4 = 16$ combinations.
  - `ShipmentBuilder(parcel).insure(500).signature().customs(form).build()`; `build()` checks rules such as "international needs a customs form".
  - In Python, keyword arguments with defaults + checks in `__post_init__` cover most cases. A Builder earns its place when construction has many steps, order matters, or rules span several parts.
  - The fluent builder is Bloch's form. The GoF Builder is broader: one construction process, several representations.

sections.title: 4. Wrapping: Adapter, Facade, Decorator, composition
sections.body:
- **Adapter**: wrap an incompatible interface so it matches the one your code expects. One foreign API → your interface.
  - Example: Postal returns JSON `{"ts": ..., "st": "DLV"}`; Courier returns XML `<event status="delivered">`.
  - Two adapters map both into one internal `TrackingEvent(at, status)`.
- **Facade**: one simple interface in front of a complex subsystem. Many parts → one call. The parts do not change.
  - Example: `ship_order(order)` hides validation, quote, booking, label, persistence and notification.
- **Decorator**: same interface, extra behavior around the call. Wraps an object or a function; stacks.
  - Example: `RetryingCarrier(TimedCarrier(PostalCarrier()))`: all three are a `Carrier`.
  - Python `@` syntax wraps a function at definition time: `@functools.cache`, `@retry`, `@timed`.
  - Order matters. The call fails twice, then succeeds:
  - `@timed` above `@retry(3)` → 1 timing record (the whole retry loop).
  - `@retry(3)` above `@timed` → 3 records (one per attempt).
- **Composition over inheritance**:
  - Inheritance couples a class to its parent's internals; deep trees get rigid.
  - Composition assembles behavior from small parts swapped at run time.
  - Example: retry, cache and timing as subclasses for every combination: $2^3 = 8$ variants per carrier × 3 carriers = **24 classes**.
  - As decorators: 3 carriers + 3 wrappers = **6 classes**, combined at run time.
- One line each: Adapter changes the interface · Decorator keeps it and adds behavior · Facade simplifies many into one.

sections.title: 5. Varying behavior: Strategy, Template method, state machines, Visitor
sections.body:
- **Strategy**: a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface; the caller picks one at run time.
  - Example: rate rules `FlatRate`, `ByWeight`, `ByZone` behind `price(parcel) -> Money`. A promotion week swaps the rule; `Quoter` does not change.
  - In Python a strategy can be a plain function passed in.
- **Template method**: a base class fixes the steps; subclasses override some (inheritance).
  - Example: `BaseCarrier.book()` = validate → request → parse → save. Subclasses override `request` and `parse`.
- Template method vs Strategy: inheritance vs composition. With Strategy the varying step is a separate object, tested alone. With Template method you need a subclass per variant.
- **Explicit state machine**: list the states and the allowed transitions; reject the rest.
```python
ALLOWED = {
    "created":       {"label_printed", "cancelled"},
    "label_printed": {"in_transit", "cancelled"},
    "in_transit":    {"delivered", "returned"},
}
```
  - `delivered → in_transit` is not in the table → rejected, logged, not silently stored.
  - Same idea: order lifecycles (new → partially filled → filled / cancelled); LangGraph graphs (state machines with LLM nodes).
  - The GoF State pattern uses one class per state. A transition table is often enough.
- **Visitor**: add operations over a fixed set of types without editing each type.
  - Double dispatch: `parcel.accept(v)` calls `v.visit_box(self)`; the call depends on both the parcel type and the visitor.
  - Example: types Letter, Box, Pallet; operations cost, label, customs as 3 visitors.
  - New operation "carbon estimate": 1 new visitor, **0** edits to existing classes.
  - New type "Tube": edit all **3** visitors.
  - Choose: types stable, operations grow → Visitor. Types grow, operations stable → methods on the types.
  - In Python, `functools.singledispatch` or `match` on the type often replaces it.

sections.title: 6. Events and requests as objects: Observer, pub-sub, Command
sections.body:
- **Observer**: the subject keeps a list of observers and calls them directly. In process, usually synchronous.
  - Example: `shipment.mark_dispatched()` calls email (120 ms), analytics (30 ms), loyalty points (50 ms).
  - → every dispatch waits **200 ms** more, and an email outage makes dispatch fail unless each call is guarded.
- **Publish-subscribe**: a broker or event bus sits between. Publishers and subscribers know only the topic.
  - Usually across processes and asynchronous. New subscribers need no change in the publisher.
  - Example: publish `ShipmentDispatched`; email, analytics and loyalty services consume it on their own. Dispatch returns once the broker accepts the message.
  - Price: brokers usually deliver **at least once** → handlers must be idempotent (dedupe by event id).
  - Writing the DB row and publishing are two steps; a crash between them loses or invents an event. A transactional outbox makes them atomic; delivery is still at least once.
- **Command**: a request as an object, e.g. `BookShipment(order_id, carrier)`.
  - It can then be queued, logged, retried or undone.
  - Example: label-print jobs queued as commands; failed ones retried; the command log is an audit trail.
  - Also: rows in a write outbox (pending work stored as data); LangGraph's `Command(update=..., goto=...)`, a node's return value that says how to change state and where to go next.
- Command vs event: a command says "do this" (one handler, can be refused). An event says "this happened" (a fact; zero or many subscribers).

sections.title: 7. Architecture: Repository, hexagonal, value objects, when to abstract
sections.body:
- **Repository**: data access behind a collection-like interface: `get(id)`, `add(shipment)`, `find(status=...)`.
  - Domain code never sees SQL or the ORM. Tests use an in-memory version (a dict).
- **Hexagonal architecture** (ports and adapters, Cockburn):
  - Core domain logic in the center, with **no IO**: quoting, the state machine, rules.
  - **Ports** = interfaces the core owns: `RateSource`, `ShipmentRepository`, `Notifier`.
  - **Adapters** plug in: Postal HTTP adapter, Postgres repository, email sender; on the driving side, the web API and a CLI.
  - Swap infrastructure (a new DB, Postal API v2) without touching the core. Core tests run with fakes in milliseconds.
  - It is dependency inversion applied to the whole system.
- **Value objects**: equality by value, no identity. `Money(cents=1250, currency="EUR")`, `Address`.
  - `@dataclass(frozen=True)`: field-wise `==`, hashable, assignment raises `FrozenInstanceError`.
  - Why: no accidental mutation through a shared reference; safe to share across threads and to use as cache keys.
  - Frozen is **shallow**: a `list` field can still change (and makes the object unhashable). Use tuples.
  - Money: integer cents or `Decimal`, never `float`.
  - Entity vs value: a `Shipment` has an id and a lifecycle (entity). `Money` and `Address` do not (values).
- **When to abstract**: DRY vs YAGNI / KISS.
  - Rule of three: write it once, tolerate one duplicate, abstract when the third copy appears.
  - Example: the Postal and Courier adapters share some parsing. Wait for Freight before extracting a base: three cases show the real common shape.
  - A wrong abstraction costs more than duplication: every caller bends to it.

sections.title: 8. Confusions to avoid
sections.body:
- Observer = pub-sub. Observer calls known objects directly, in process. Pub-sub goes through a broker; parties know only the topic.
- "Pub-sub delivers exactly once." Usually at least once → idempotent handlers. An outbox gives atomic publish, still at least once.
- Adapter vs Facade vs Decorator: changes the interface · simplifies many into one · same interface + behavior.
- "Every Python `@` is the Decorator pattern." `@dataclass` and `@property` transform; `@app.route` registers.
- Dependency inversion = dependency injection. Principle vs technique. You can inject a concrete class and still depend on it.
- "Singleton = one instance." The harm is the global access point, not the count.
- Template method vs Strategy: inheritance vs composition.
- "Visitor makes new types cheap." The opposite: new operations are cheap, new types touch every visitor.
- "Every optional argument needs a Builder." In Python, keyword arguments with defaults come first.
- LSP is about behavior, not signatures. A subclass that raises on a base method breaks it.
- ISP vs SRP: ISP is about what a **client** depends on; SRP is about why a **module** changes.
- `frozen=True` = deep immutability. It is shallow.
- Command vs event: "do this" vs "this happened".
- Abstracting at the second copy. Wait for the third.

sd-08-patterns.summary:
### SOLID
- S one reason to change · O add a class, not an `elif` · L subtype never surprises · I small role interfaces · D core owns the interfaces.
### Dependencies
- Inversion = principle; injection = technique.
- `Protocol` structural · `ABC` nominal.
- Singleton harm = global access → create at startup, inject.
### Create
- Factory picks the concrete type. Builder: many optional parts, validate in `build()`.
### Wrap
- Adapter changes interface · Facade one entry point · Decorator same interface + behavior.
- Subclass per combination = $2^k$ per class; decorators = $k$ wrappers.
- Outer decorator runs around everything inside it.
### Vary
- Strategy (object passed in) vs Template method (subclass).
- State machine: table of allowed transitions.
- Visitor: new operation 0 edits; new type edits every visitor.
### Events
- Observer direct + in process · pub-sub broker + topic, at least once → idempotent.
- Command = request as object: queue, log, retry, undo.
### Architecture
- Repository hides SQL. Hexagonal: core + ports; adapters outside.
- Value object: frozen, equal by value, shallow. Rule of three.

questions.stem: `ShipmentService` quotes prices, calls the carrier APIs, renders the PDF label and emails the customer. A label layout change forces a re-test of pricing. Which principle is broken, and what is the fix?

options.t: Single responsibility: four reasons to change in one module; split it into four parts
options.why: Pricing rules, carrier API, label layout and email text change for different people at different times.

options.t: Open/closed: add a subclass per label layout
options.why: OCP is about adding variants without edits. The problem here is unrelated jobs in one module.

options.t: Liskov substitution: the service cannot replace its base class
options.why: No subtype is involved.

options.t: Wrap it in a Facade
options.why: A facade hides complexity behind one call. The four jobs would still live and change together.

questions.stem: Three carriers are handled by `if/elif` chains in 4 functions: `quote`, `book`, `track`, `cancel`. You add a 4th carrier. How many **existing** functions do you edit with the chains, and with one class per carrier plus a factory registry?

options.t: 4 with the chains; 0 with classes (1 new class + 1 registry line)
options.why: Each chain needs a new branch. With polymorphism the new code lives in one new class.

options.t: 3 with the chains; 1 with classes
options.why: That counts carriers, not the functions that hold a chain.

options.t: 12 with the chains; 4 with classes
options.why: 12 is the number of branches today (3 × 4). The new class has 4 methods, but no existing code changes.

options.t: 4 in both designs
options.why: The new class implements 4 methods, but none of them is an edit to existing code.

questions.stem: A nightly report loops over all carriers and calls `c.track(id)`. `FreightCarrier(Carrier)` raises `NotImplementedError` in `track()`, and the report crashes. Which principle does `FreightCarrier` violate?

options.t: Liskov substitution: it cannot stand in for `Carrier` without surprising callers
options.why: Fix: a separate `Trackable` role, or a contract result such as "no tracking".

options.t: Interface segregation
options.why: Splitting the interface is a good fix, but the violation itself is broken substitutability.

options.t: Open/closed
options.why: Nothing had to be edited to add Freight; the problem is how it behaves.

options.t: Dependency inversion
options.why: The report depends on the `Carrier` abstraction, as DIP asks.

questions.stem: `Quoter.__init__` does `self.client = PostalHttpClient.instance()`. Its unit tests are slow and flaky because they call the real carrier. Best fix?

options.t: Let `Quoter` take a `RateSource` (a Protocol it owns) in its constructor; pass a fake in tests and the HTTP adapter in production
options.why: Dependency inversion + injection: the core no longer knows the IO class.

options.t: `mock.patch` `PostalHttpClient.instance` in every test
options.why: It works, but treats the symptom: the core still depends on a concrete IO class through a global.

options.t: Make the singleton thread-safe
options.why: Threading is not the problem. Hidden global IO is.

options.t: Replace the singleton with a module-level client object
options.why: Same global state under another name.

questions.stem: 3 carriers. Each may need any combination of retry, caching and timing. How many classes if every combination is a subclass, and how many with decorators?

options.t: 24 subclasses; 6 classes with decorators
options.why: $2^3 = 8$ variants per carrier × 3 = 24. Decorators: 3 carriers + 3 wrappers, combined at run time.

options.t: 9 subclasses; 6 with decorators
options.why: 3 × 3 counts each option once. Combinations multiply: each option is on or off.

options.t: 8 subclasses; 3 with decorators
options.why: That is one carrier only. There are three.

options.t: 24 in both designs
options.why: Decorators combine at run time, so no class per combination is needed.

questions.stem: Postal returns tracking as JSON `{"ts", "st"}`; Courier returns XML. The rest of the code should see one `TrackingEvent(at, status)`. Which pattern?

options.t: Adapter: one per carrier, mapping its format into `TrackingEvent`
options.why: Adapter converts a foreign interface into the one your code expects.

options.t: Facade
options.why: A facade puts one simple call in front of many parts. It does not translate one interface into another.

options.t: Decorator
options.why: A decorator keeps the same interface and adds behavior. Here the interfaces differ.

options.t: Strategy
options.why: Strategy swaps algorithms behind an interface you already have; it does not convert formats.

questions.stem: `mark_dispatched()` notifies email (120 ms), analytics (30 ms) and loyalty (50 ms) observers directly. Dispatch got 200 ms slower and fails when the email server is down. What is the fix, and what does it cost?

options.t: Publish a `ShipmentDispatched` event to a broker; consumers subscribe. Cost: at-least-once delivery, so handlers must be idempotent
options.why: Pub-sub decouples the publisher in time and failure. The broker may redeliver.

options.t: Nothing to change in the design: Observer and pub-sub are the same pattern; add a timeout
options.why: Observer calls known objects directly, in process. Pub-sub puts a broker between them.

options.t: Switch to pub-sub; it guarantees exactly-once delivery, so no other change is needed
options.why: Most brokers deliver at least once. Duplicate events must be harmless.

options.t: Wrap each notification in a Command object
options.why: A command makes a request queueable, but calling it inline still blocks dispatch.

questions.stem: `fetch_rate` is decorated with `@timed` on top and `@retry(3)` below it. The call fails twice, then succeeds. How many timing records, and how many if the order is swapped?

options.t: 1 here; 3 if swapped
options.why: The outer decorator wraps everything inside it. `@timed` outside times the whole retry loop; inside, it times each attempt.

options.t: 3 here; 1 if swapped
options.why: Reversed: the top decorator is the outermost wrapper.

options.t: 3 in both orders
options.why: Order matters: decorators nest.

options.t: 1 in both orders
options.why: With `@timed` inside the retry, each attempt is timed.

questions.stem: To test a new rate rule, the team must subclass `BaseQuoter` and stub its five other steps. What refactor helps most?

options.t: Strategy: pass the rate rule in as an object or function; test it alone
options.why: Template method ties the varying step to the base class. Strategy isolates it.

options.t: Add another level of inheritance for test subclasses
options.why: Deeper trees make the coupling worse.

options.t: Visitor
options.why: Visitor adds operations over a fixed set of types. The problem is one varying step.

options.t: Factory
options.why: A factory picks which object to create; it does not separate the varying step from the fixed ones.

questions.stem: Parcel types Letter, Box, Pallet; operations cost, label, customs as 3 Visitor classes. How many existing classes do you edit to add the operation "carbon estimate", and to add the type "Tube"?

options.t: 0 for the operation; 3 for the type
options.why: A new operation is a new visitor. A new type needs a `visit_tube` in each of the 3 visitors.

options.t: 3 for the operation; 0 for the type
options.why: That is the plain-methods design (operations live on the types), the opposite trade-off.

options.t: 1 and 1
options.why: Visitor makes one kind of change cheap and the other one costly.

options.t: 3 and 3
options.why: Adding an operation adds a class; it edits none.

questions.stem: Two shipments share one `Money` object as their base fee. Insurance code does `fee.cents += 200`, and both shipments change. Best fix?

options.t: Make `Money` a frozen value object and return a new instance: `fee = fee.add(Money(200, "EUR"))`
options.why: Immutable values cannot change under a shared reference. Equality stays by value.

options.t: `copy.deepcopy` the fee before every use
options.why: Works where you remember it. Immutability removes the whole class of bug.

options.t: Give each `Money` an id, so two fees are never equal
options.why: That makes money an entity. Two EUR 2.00 amounts should be equal.

options.t: Add a lock around the fee
options.why: This is aliasing in one thread, not a race between threads.

questions.stem: Explain hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters) for the shipping service: what sits in the core, what are the ports and adapters, how tests run, and how it relates to dependency inversion.
questions.answer: The core holds domain logic with no IO: quoting, the shipment state machine, business rules. It owns ports, i.e. interfaces such as RateSource, ShipmentRepository and Notifier. Adapters outside implement them: carrier HTTP clients, a Postgres repository, an email sender; driving adapters (web API, CLI) call into the core. Source dependencies point inward, which is dependency inversion at system scale. Tests run the core with in-memory fakes, fast and without network, and infrastructure can be swapped without touching the core.

llm-02-training.title: Training and adaptation: from base model to assistant
llm-02-training.source: Kaplan et al. 2020 (Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models); Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla), eq. 10, Tables 2–3; Meta, Llama 3 announcement (2024); Ouyang et al. 2022 (InstructGPT); Rafailov et al. 2023 (DPO), eqs. 1, 3, 7; Shao et al. 2024 (DeepSeekMath, GRPO); Hu et al. 2021 (LoRA); Dettmers et al. 2023 (QLoRA); Hinton, Vinyals & Dean 2015 (distillation); Kalai et al. 2025 (Why Language Models Hallucinate); LoRA defaults checked with peft 0.17.1
llm-02-training.intro:
Student notes. One example runs to the end: a lab builds **Tutor**, a math-tutoring assistant.
Path: pretrain a 70B base model → teach it to follow instructions (SFT) → align it to preferences → train it on checkable math answers → adapt it cheaply (LoRA, QLoRA) → shrink it for serving (distillation to an 8B student, quantization).
Shapes follow the public Llama 3 configs (70B: 80 layers, width 8192; 8B: width 4096). All other numbers are illustrative.

objectives.text: what each training stage adds: pretraining, SFT, preference tuning and RL with verifiable rewards
training compute ($C \approx 6ND$) and the compute-optimal split between parameters and tokens
RLHF with PPO, DPO and GRPO: what each needs and what it optimizes
LoRA trainable parameters and fine-tuning memory for full, LoRA and QLoRA training
quantization and distillation; prompting, RAG and fine-tuning
training failures: reward hacking, groups with no learning signal, and hallucination rewarded by grading

sections.title: 1. Pretraining: next-token prediction
sections.body:
- Task: predict the next token over a huge corpus. Loss = $-\ln p(\text{correct token})$, averaged over positions (see the LLM 01 note).
- Scale: Llama 3 trained on over 15T tokens.
- What it learns: language, facts, patterns, some reasoning.
- What it does not learn: to follow instructions, to stop, to say "I don't know".
- Example. Prompt to the Tutor base model: `Q: What is 7 × 8?\nA:`
  - It may answer `56`, then write `Q: What is 9 × 6?` and go on.
  - It continues the document. A quiz page usually has more questions.
- → the base model **completes text**. The later stages turn it into an assistant.

sections.title: 2. Scaling laws and the compute budget
sections.body:
- **Scaling laws** (Kaplan 2020): loss falls as a **power law** in parameters $N$, tokens $D$ and compute $C$, if the other two do not bind.
- Chinchilla fit (Hoffmann 2022, eq. 10):
$$L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}}$$
  - $E = 1.69$ (the floor), $A = 406.4$, $B = 410.7$, $\alpha = 0.34$, $\beta = 0.28$.
  - Tutor-70B on 1.4T tokens: $L \approx 1.937$.
  - Each 4× of compute (2× $N$, 2× $D$): 1.937 → 1.890 → 1.853 → 1.822. Each step buys less.
- **Compute**: $C \approx 6ND$ FLOPs.
  - 2 per parameter per token for the forward pass, 4 for the backward pass.
  - Tutor: $6 \times 70 \times 10^{9} \times 1.4 \times 10^{12} \approx 5.9 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs.
- **Compute-optimal** (Chinchilla): grow $N$ and $D$ together, each about $\propto C^{0.5}$.
  - Rule of thumb: **≈ 20 tokens per parameter**. 70B → 1.4T tokens (Chinchilla itself). Table 3: 10B → 205B tokens.
  - 4× compute → 2× parameters and 2× tokens, not 4× parameters.
  - The parametric fit leans a bit more to data ($N \propto C^{0.46}$, $D \propto C^{0.54}$).
- Time: H100 dense bf16 = 989 TFLOPS. At 40% utilization: $5.9 \times 10^{23} / (0.4 \times 989 \times 10^{12}) \approx 1.5 \times 10^{9}$ GPU-seconds ≈ 17,200 GPU-days → **1,000 GPUs for about 17 days**.
- **Over-training** on purpose: Llama 3 8B saw 15T tokens, about 1,900 per parameter. Chinchilla-optimal is about 200B tokens.
  - Why: inference cost grows with $N$. A smaller model trained longer is cheaper to serve for its whole life.

sections.title: 3. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
sections.body:
- SFT = train on **demonstrations**: prompt → ideal response. Same next-token loss as pretraining.
- The loss usually counts only the response tokens. The prompt is context, not a target.
- Dialogues follow a **chat template**: special tokens mark system, user and assistant turns, and the end of a turn.
- It teaches format and instruction following: answer the question, show the steps, then stop.
- Example: 20,000 tutor dialogues × 1,000 tokens = 20M tokens. That is 1/70,000 of the 1.4T pretraining tokens.
- → SFT changes **behavior**. The knowledge comes almost all from pretraining.
- Limit: the model copies the demonstrations. It cannot get better than them, and it learns nothing from comparing two answers.

sections.title: 4. Preference tuning: RLHF and DPO
sections.body:
- Data: a prompt and two answers; a human marks the better one ($y_w$ wins, $y_l$ loses).
- **RLHF** (InstructGPT recipe):
  1. Humans compare pairs of responses.
  2. A **reward model** learns the preferences. Bradley–Terry: $P(y_1 \succ y_2) = \sigma(r_1 - r_2)$.
  3. The policy is optimized with RL (PPO) to maximize reward, with a KL penalty to a reference model (the SFT model).
- Objective (DPO paper, eq. 3):
$$\max_{\pi_\theta}\; \mathbb{E}[r(x, y)] - \beta\, \mathrm{KL}\left[\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}\right]$$
- Example: the reward model scores Tutor answer A at 1.2 and B at 0.2 → $P(A \succ B) = \sigma(1.0) \approx 0.73$.
- **Why the KL penalty**: the reward model is an imperfect proxy. Without the leash, the policy drifts and finds its flaws (**reward hacking**).
  - Example: the reward model likes long answers → Tutor learns to pad every answer.
- **DPO**: no reward model, no RL loop. A classification-style loss on the pairs (eq. 7):
$$\mathcal{L} = -\ln \sigma\left(\beta \ln \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w)} - \beta \ln \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l)}\right)$$
  - At the start $\pi_\theta = \pi_{\text{ref}}$: margin 0 → $\mathcal{L} = \ln 2 \approx 0.693$.
  - Example, $\beta = 0.1$: log-ratio of the winner +2, of the loser −3 → margin $0.1 \times 5 = 0.5$ → $\mathcal{L} = -\ln \sigma(0.5) \approx 0.474$.
  - The loss pushes the winner up and the loser down, **relative to the reference**. $\beta$ plays the role of the KL weight.
- Trade-off: DPO is simpler and more stable. RLHF samples fresh answers during training, so it can explore beyond the fixed pairs.

sections.title: 5. RL with verifiable rewards and GRPO
sections.body:
- **RLVR**: RL on tasks whose answer a program can check. The checker is the reward.
  - Math: final answer = answer key → 1, else 0. Code: unit tests pass → 1.
  - No human labels and no learned reward model → it scales. Central to reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1).
- **PPO** needs a value (critic) model, usually as large as the policy, to estimate a baseline.
- **GRPO** (DeepSeekMath) drops the critic. For each prompt:
  1. Sample a group of $G$ answers.
  2. Score each one.
  3. Advantage = (reward − group mean) / group std.
$$\hat{A}_i = \frac{r_i - \operatorname{mean}(r)}{\operatorname{std}(r)}$$
- Example: Tutor answers one problem $G = 4$ times; rewards $[1, 0, 0, 1]$.
  - Mean 0.5, std 0.5 → advantages $[+1, -1, -1, +1]$.
  - Right answers become more likely, wrong ones less likely.
  - Code that uses the sample std ($n - 1$) gives ±0.87: same signs, same order.
- The KL to the reference goes **into the loss**, not into the reward.
- **No signal**: if all 4 answers are right (or all wrong), std = 0 and every advantage is 0. Code usually adds a small ε to the std. The prompt teaches nothing → too-easy and too-hard prompts waste compute.
- **Reward hacking** still happens if the checker is weak.
  - Example: the checker accepts an answer if the key number appears anywhere. Tutor learns to list several candidate numbers.
  - Fix the checker: parse one final answer in a fixed format.

sections.title: 6. LoRA and QLoRA
sections.body:
- Full fine-tuning updates every weight. With Adam in mixed precision: **16 bytes per parameter** = bf16 weights 2 + gradients 2 + fp32 master weights 4 + Adam moments 8.
  - Tutor-70B: $70 \times 10^{9} \times 16$ = **1.12 TB** before activations → at least 14 H100s just to hold it.
- **LoRA**: freeze $W$; learn a low-rank update.
$$W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r} BA, \quad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r},\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$$
  - Trainable: $r(d + k)$ instead of $dk$.
  - Example: a 4096×4096 projection (the width of the 8B model), $r = 8$: $2 \times 4096 \times 8 = 65{,}536$ parameters = **0.39%** of 16.8M.
  - Whole Tutor-70B, $r = 8$ on the query and value projections of all 80 layers: 16.4M trainable = 0.023%.
  - $B$ starts at zero → at step 0 the model equals the base model.
  - peft 0.17.1 defaults: $r = 8$, $\alpha = 8$ (scale 1).
  - The bet: the fine-tuning update has low rank.
- Memory with LoRA: gradients and Adam states only for the adapters (16.4M × 16 B ≈ 0.26 GB). The frozen base remains: **140 GB** in bf16.
- After training, merge: $W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$ → no extra inference cost. Or keep several small adapters on one base.
- **QLoRA**: the frozen base in **4-bit NF4**; adapters train in bf16.
  - Base: $70 \times 10^{9} \times 0.5$ B = **35 GB**, 4× less than bf16.
  - One scale per block of 64 weights. Double quantization (quantize the scales too) cuts their cost from 0.5 to 0.127 bits per parameter: ≈ 1.1 GB for 70B.
  - The paper fine-tunes a 65B model on one 48 GB GPU.

sections.title: 7. Shrinking for serving: quantization and distillation
sections.body:
- **Quantization**: store weights (and sometimes activations) in fewer bits.
  - 70B: bf16 140 GB · int8/fp8 70 GB · int4 35 GB.
  - Less memory and faster decode (fewer bytes to read per token, LLM 05 note), for a small quality loss.
- Absmax int8 on a block $w = [0.12, -0.50, 0.03, 0.31]$:
  - Scale $s = 0.50/127 \approx 0.00394$. Store $\text{round}(w/s) = [30, -127, 8, 79]$.
  - Read back $q \cdot s = [0.118, -0.500, 0.031, 0.311]$. Error ≤ $s/2$.
- **Outliers** break it: add 8.0 to the block → $s = 8/127 \approx 0.063$ → 0.03 rounds to 0. Hence small blocks, each with its own scale.
- **Distillation**: a small **student** learns to match a large **teacher**'s output probabilities (soft targets), not only the right token.
  - Example: teacher on `7 × 8 =`: 56 → 0.90, 54 → 0.06, 48 → 0.04. The soft targets say 54 is the nearer mistake; a one-hot label does not.
  - Tutor-8B, distilled from Tutor-70B: 16 GB in bf16, 8.75× fewer bytes per token than the teacher. It keeps much of the quality.
- They stack: distill to 8B, then int4 → about 4 GB.
- Quantization keeps the network and cuts bits. Distillation trains a new, smaller network.

sections.title: 8. Hallucination, and which tool to use
sections.body:
- **Hallucination**: a fluent, confident, wrong answer.
- Why: training rewards plausible continuations, not calibrated "I don't know". Most evals grade right/wrong; under that scoring, guessing beats abstaining (Kalai et al. 2025).
- Example: Tutor is 30% sure of an answer.
  - Binary grading: guess → expected score 0.3; abstain → 0. It guesses.
  - Confidence target $t = 0.75$: a wrong answer costs $t/(1-t) = 3$ points. Guess → $0.3 - 0.7 \times 3 = -1.8$. It abstains.
  - In general, guessing pays only when $p > t$.
- Mitigations: ground with retrieval, cite sources, use tools (a calculator for arithmetic), reward abstention in training and evals.
- **Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning**:
  - Prompting first: cheap, fast to change.
  - RAG: knowledge that changes or is private. Example: this term's syllabus and exercise sheets.
  - Fine-tuning: stable behavior, style or format at scale. Example: Tutor's step-by-step hint format on every answer.
  - Fine-tuning is a poor way to add fresh facts: hard to update, and the model can still mix them up. Fresh facts → RAG.

sections.title: 9. Where I get confused
sections.body:
- Pretraining gives knowledge, not obedience. A base model continues the document.
- $C \approx 6ND$, not $2ND$: $2ND$ is the forward pass only (that is the inference cost per token × tokens).
- Compute-optimal is not "biggest model". 4× compute → 2× $N$ and 2× $D$.
- Over-training a small model is not a mistake. It trades extra training compute for cheaper inference.
- The KL term is not a regularizer for overfitting the data. It stops the policy exploiting the reward model.
- DPO still uses a reference model. It drops the reward model and the RL loop, not $\pi_{\text{ref}}$.
- GRPO drops the **critic**, not the reward. A group where every answer scores the same teaches nothing.
- LoRA cuts the trainable states, not the frozen base weights. 70B LoRA still holds 140 GB of base in bf16.
- LoRA params = $r(d + k)$, not $r^2$ and not $d \times r$.
- QLoRA quantizes the frozen base, not the adapters.
- Quantization ≠ distillation: same network with fewer bits vs a new smaller network.
- Fine-tuning for fresh facts → use RAG.

llm-02-training.summary:
### Stages
- Pretrain (next token) → SFT (demonstrations) → preferences (RLHF or DPO) → RLVR (checkable answers).
### Scaling
- $L = E + A/N^{0.34} + B/D^{0.28}$: power law, diminishing gains.
- $C \approx 6ND$. 70B × 1.4T ≈ $5.9 \times 10^{23}$.
- Compute-optimal ≈ 20 tokens/param; 4× compute → 2× N, 2× D.
### Preferences
- Bradley–Terry: $P(A \succ B) = \sigma(r_A - r_B)$.
- RLHF: reward model + PPO + KL to reference.
- DPO: $-\ln\sigma(\beta\,\Delta\text{log-ratio})$; starts at $\ln 2$.
- GRPO: $\hat A = (r - \text{mean})/\text{std}$ over $G$ samples; no critic; equal rewards → no signal.
### Adapt
- Full FT: 16 B/param → 70B ≈ 1.12 TB.
- LoRA: $r(d+k)$ params; 4096², r 8 → 65,536 (0.39%). Base stays: 140 GB.
- QLoRA: base in NF4 → 35 GB + ≈ 1 GB scales.
### Shrink
- Quantize: fewer bits, same net. Distill: smaller net learns teacher's probabilities.
### Choose
- Prompt → RAG (fresh/private facts) → fine-tune (behavior, format).
- Guess only if $p > t$ when wrong costs $t/(1-t)$.

questions.stem: You prompt the Tutor base model (pretraining only) with `Q: What is 7 × 8?\nA:`. It answers `56`, then writes three more quiz questions. What explains this?

options.t: It is a base model: it continues the document; following instructions and stopping come from SFT
options.why: Pretraining teaches next-token prediction. A quiz page usually has more questions, so the model writes them.

options.t: The temperature is too high
options.why: Temperature changes how random each token is. Greedy decoding would still continue the quiz.

options.t: The model lacks the knowledge; it needs RLHF to learn arithmetic
options.why: It got 56 right. The missing part is behavior, not knowledge, and preference tuning does not add facts.

options.t: The context window is too short
options.why: The prompt is a few tokens. Length is not the issue.

questions.stem: About how many FLOPs does it take to train Tutor-70B on 1.4T tokens?

options.t: About $5.9 \times 10^{23}$
options.why: $C \approx 6ND = 6 \times 70 \times 10^{9} \times 1.4 \times 10^{12}$.

options.t: About $2.0 \times 10^{23}$
options.why: That is $2ND$: the forward pass only. The backward pass costs about twice the forward.

options.t: About $9.8 \times 10^{22}$
options.why: That is $N \times D$ without the factor 6.

options.t: About $5.9 \times 10^{21}$
options.why: Off by 100×: $70 \times 10^{9} \times 1.4 \times 10^{12} \approx 10^{23}$ before the factor 6.

questions.stem: The lab gets 4× the compute of the Tutor-70B run (70B, 1.4T tokens). Following Chinchilla, how should it spend it?

options.t: About 140B parameters on 2.8T tokens
options.why: $N$ and $D$ grow together, each about $\propto C^{0.5}$: 2 × 2 = 4× compute, still ≈ 20 tokens per parameter.

options.t: About 280B parameters on 1.4T tokens
options.why: All the compute into parameters: the pre-Chinchilla habit. The model ends up under-trained (5 tokens per parameter).

options.t: About 280B parameters on 5.6T tokens
options.why: 4× both is 16× the compute, since $C \approx 6ND$.

options.t: 70B parameters on 5.6T tokens, always
options.why: Over-training can pay off for inference cost, but it is not the compute-optimal split for training loss.

questions.stem: DPO with $\beta = 0.1$. After some training, the policy's log-ratio vs the reference is +2 on the winning answer and −3 on the losing one. What is the loss on this pair?

options.t: About 0.474
About 0.693
options.why: That is $\ln 2$, the loss at the start, when policy = reference and the margin is 0.

options.t: About 0.0067
options.why: That drops $\beta$: $-\ln\sigma(5)$.

options.t: About 0.974
options.why: That flips the sign of the margin: $-\ln\sigma(-0.5)$. The winner's term enters with a plus.

questions.stem: After RLHF with a very small KL weight, Tutor's reward-model score keeps rising, but human raters say answers got worse: long, padded, full of praise. Diagnosis?

options.t: Reward hacking: the policy drifted far from the reference and exploits flaws of the reward model
options.why: The reward model is a proxy. The KL penalty keeps the policy near the reference; with almost none, it optimizes the proxy's flaws.

options.t: Overfitting of the SFT data
options.why: SFT copies demonstrations; it does not push a score up while quality falls.

options.t: Hallucination from pretraining
options.why: The change came with RL and tracks the reward score, not missing knowledge.

options.t: The learning rate is too low
options.why: A low rate slows change. Here the policy changed a lot, in the wrong direction.

questions.stem: GRPO, group of $G = 4$ answers to one problem, rewards $[1, 0, 0, 1]$. What advantages does the paper's formula give?

options.why: That subtracts the mean but does not divide by the std.
Raw rewards with no baseline: wrong answers would get no push down.

options.t: It needs a value model to estimate the baseline
options.why: That is PPO. GRPO uses the group mean as the baseline.

questions.stem: In GRPO training, half of the prompts get 4 out of 4 correct answers every time. What do those prompts contribute?

options.t: Nothing: equal rewards → std 0 → every advantage is 0, so no gradient
options.why: With a small ε added to the std, the advantages are exactly 0. Too-easy prompts waste the sampling compute.

options.t: A strong positive update, since every answer is right
options.why: Advantages are relative to the group. All equal → no answer beats the mean.

options.t: A strong negative update from the KL term
options.why: The KL term keeps the policy near the reference; it does not turn correct answers into a penalty.

options.t: The same signal as a group with one right answer
options.why: A group with one right answer has spread: that answer gets a large positive advantage.

questions.stem: LoRA with rank $r = 16$ on one 4096×4096 projection. How many trainable parameters?

options.t: 131,072 (0.78% of the matrix)

options.why: That is $r = 8$, or only one of the two factors at $r = 16$.
That is $r^2$. $B$ is $d \times r$ and $A$ is $r \times k$.
That is the full matrix $W$, which LoRA freezes.

questions.stem: Tutor-70B. Memory for weights plus training states (no activations): full fine-tuning with Adam in mixed precision, LoRA, and QLoRA?

options.why: Full: 16 B/param. LoRA: frozen bf16 base (2 B/param) plus tiny adapter states. QLoRA: 4-bit base (0.5 B/param) plus ≈ 1 GB of scales.
Full fine-tuning also stores gradients, fp32 master weights and two Adam moments.
LoRA needs gradients and Adam states only for the adapters, under 0.1% of the parameters.
That counts only the adapter states. The frozen base must still sit in memory.

questions.stem: After RLVR, Tutor's math accuracy on the training checker is 95%, but teachers say answers now end with lines like "the answer is 12, or 14, or 16". Most likely cause?

options.t: Reward hacking: the checker accepts the answer if the key appears anywhere, so listing candidates scores
options.why: RLVR optimizes the checker. Fix the checker: parse one final answer in a fixed format.

options.t: The KL weight is too high
options.why: A high KL weight holds the policy near the reference; it does not invent a new answer pattern.

options.t: The model hallucinates from missing knowledge
options.why: The pattern appeared with the RL reward and scores well on it. It is learned, not missing knowledge.

options.t: The group size is too small
options.why: Small groups give noisier advantages, not a systematic trick.

questions.stem: Tutor is 30% sure of an answer. The eval states: answer only if more than 75% confident; a wrong answer costs 3 points, a right one earns 1, "I don't know" earns 0. Best action and why?

options.t: Abstain: guessing has expected score $0.3 - 0.7 \times 3 = -1.8$
options.why: With penalty $t/(1-t)$, guessing pays only when $p > t$. Here $0.3 < 0.75$.

options.t: Guess: expected score 0.3 beats 0
options.why: That is binary grading, where a wrong answer costs nothing. This eval penalizes mistakes.

options.t: Guess: a 30% chance is better than zero
options.why: Ignores the 70% chance of losing 3 points.

options.t: Abstain: the expected score of guessing is −0.4
options.why: That uses a penalty of 1 point ($t = 0.5$), not 3.

questions.stem: Tutor must (a) use this term's syllabus and exercise sheets, which change every few weeks, and (b) always answer in the house hint-first format. Compare prompting, RAG and fine-tuning for each need.
questions.answer: Start with prompting for both: it is cheap and fast to change. (a) The syllabus is changing, private knowledge: use RAG, which retrieves the current sheets at answer time; fine-tuning would need retraining at each change and the model could still mix old and new facts. (b) A fixed format on every answer is stable behavior: if the prompt alone is not reliable or costs too many tokens at scale, fine-tune (SFT, cheaply with LoRA) on examples in that format.

llm-05-inference.title: Inference: memory, bandwidth and GPU sizing
llm-05-inference.source: Llama 3 70B and 8B config.json (layers, heads, KV heads; parameter counts checked with transformers 4.57.6); NVIDIA H100 product page (H100 SXM: 80 GB, 3.35 TB/s, 1,979 TFLOPS bf16 with sparsity = 989 dense, NVLink 900 GB/s); Kwon et al. 2023 (vLLM, PagedAttention); Yu et al. 2022 (Orca); Leviathan et al. 2023 (speculative decoding), eq. 1; Mistral AI 2023 (Mixtral of experts); Rajbhandari et al. 2020 (ZeRO); Shoeybi et al. 2019 (Megatron-LM); roofline model
llm-05-inference.intro:
Student notes. One example runs to the end: serve a **Llama-3-70B-style model** to **32 users at once, each with up to 8k tokens of context**, in bf16, on NVIDIA H100 SXM GPUs.
Model shape (public config): 80 layers, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, ≈ 70.6B parameters (we round to 70B).
GPU: 80 GB, 3.35 TB/s memory bandwidth, 989 TFLOPS dense bf16.
Question of the note: how many GPUs, how fast per user, and which lever to pull when it does not fit?

objectives.text: why the KV cache works, and how prefill and decode differ
weight and KV-cache memory, and the number of GPUs needed to serve a model
decode speed from memory bandwidth, and the batch size where compute becomes the limit
static and continuous batching, PagedAttention, tensor and pipeline parallelism
prompt caching, speculative decoding and quantization: what each saves, and whether the output changes
out-of-memory and slow serving, and pick the right lever

sections.title: 1. Prefill, decode and the KV cache
sections.body:
- Generation has two phases:
  1. **Prefill**: the whole prompt in one parallel pass. Fills the KV cache. Bound by **compute**. Sets the time to first token.
  2. **Decode**: one token per step. Each step reads all the weights and the cache. Bound by **memory bandwidth**. Sets the time per output token.
- Forward cost ≈ $2N$ FLOPs per token (training is $6N$: see the LLM 02 note).
  - Example: a 6,000-token prompt → $2 \times 70 \times 10^{9} \times 6{,}000 = 8.4 \times 10^{14}$ FLOPs → ≈ 0.2 s on 4 H100s at full speed.
- **Why the KV cache is possible**: with the causal mask, a token's K and V depend only on itself and earlier tokens. New tokens never change them → compute once, store.
  - Frozen weights alone are not enough: in a bidirectional encoder, a new token would change the old tokens' vectors.
- **What it saves**: recomputing K and V of the whole prefix at every step. Each step runs the projections and the MLP for the new token only.
- **What it costs**: GPU memory, linear in context length and in the number of concurrent sequences. Attention still **reads** every cached token at each step.

sections.title: 2. Memory for weights
sections.body:
- Rule: **parameters × bytes per parameter**.
  - bf16/fp16: 2 bytes · int8/fp8: 1 · int4: 0.5.
- Example, 70B:
  - bf16: **140 GB** · fp8: 70 GB · int4: 35 GB (plus a little for scales).
  - One H100 has 80 GB → the bf16 weights alone need 2 GPUs.
- **MoE** (mixture of experts): a router sends each token to a few experts.
  - Memory follows **total** parameters: every expert must be loaded.
  - Compute per token follows **active** parameters.
  - Example: Mixtral 8x7B has 46.7B total, 12.9B used per token (2 of 8 experts). bf16 weights ≈ 93 GB; compute per token like a 13B dense model.
- Training needs far more than serving (section 7): 16 bytes per parameter with Adam.

sections.title: 3. KV-cache size
sections.body:
- Bytes per token:
$$2 \times L \times h_{kv} \times d_{head} \times b$$
  - 2 for K and V · $L$ layers · $h_{kv}$ KV heads · $d_{head}$ head dimension · $b$ bytes per value.
- Total = per token × context length × concurrent sequences.
- Example: $2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 327{,}680$ bytes = **320 KiB per token**.
  - One user at 8,192 tokens: **2.5 GiB**.
  - 32 users: **80 GiB ≈ 86 GB**. More than one H100, before any weights.
- **GQA** pays off here: with 64 KV heads (one per query head) the cache would be 8× larger: 2.5 MiB per token, 640 GiB for the 32 users.
- Levers that shrink KV **per token or per sequence**:
  1. Fewer KV heads (GQA/MQA) or a compressed KV (MLA). Built into the model.
  2. KV quantization: fp8 halves it → ≈ 43 GB for the 32 users.
  3. Shorter context, or sliding-window attention.
- Paged allocation (section 6) cuts **waste**, not the size per token.

sections.title: 4. Sizing the GPUs
sections.body:
- Sum: weights + KV + overhead (activations, CUDA context, fragmentation; ~10–20%).
- Example: 140 GB + 86 GB = 226 GB → with overhead ≈ 250–270 GB.
  - 3 H100s = 240 GB: too tight. → **4 H100s (320 GB)** with tensor parallelism.
  - Per GPU: 35 GB of weights + 21.5 GB of KV ≈ 57 GB, out of 80.
  - Tensor parallelism splits the heads evenly: 64 heads split over 2, 4 or 8 GPUs, not 3.
- If it does not fit, the levers:
  - Quantize weights: int4 → 35 + 86 ≈ 121 GB → 2 H100s.
  - Quantize KV: fp8 → 140 + 43 ≈ 183 GB.
  - Fewer concurrent users, or a shorter context.
  - A bigger GPU: 2 × H200 = 282 GB ≥ ≈ 250 GB, but tight.
- GPU memory to remember:
  - A100: 40 or 80 GB · H100: 80 GB · H200: 141 GB.
  - B200: 180 GB usable (192 GB physical) · B300: 288 GB.
  - L4 and RTX 4090: 24 GB.

sections.title: 5. Decode speed: bandwidth and the roofline
sections.body:
- One decode step reads **every weight once**. With one sequence, that read dominates.
- Ceiling: tokens/s per sequence ≈ bandwidth / bytes read per step.
  - Llama-3-8B, bf16 (16 GB), one H100: $3.35 \text{ TB/s} / 16 \text{ GB} \approx 210$ tokens/s.
  - Our 70B on 4 H100s (13.4 TB/s together): $13.4 / 0.14 \approx$ **96 tokens/s**. Real numbers are lower (communication, kernels).
  - int4 weights (35 GB): ≈ 383 tokens/s. Quantization speeds decode, not only memory.
- **Batching** reuses each weight read for every sequence in the batch.
  - Per token, a 2-byte weight gives 2 FLOPs (multiply-add): **1 FLOP per byte** per sequence. A batch of $B$ → $B$ FLOPs/byte.
  - H100: $989 \text{ TFLOPS} / 3.35 \text{ TB/s} \approx 295$ FLOPs/byte → weights stop being the bottleneck near $B \approx 300$.
- But the **KV cache is per sequence**: its reads grow with $B$ and keep attention bandwidth-bound.
  - Example: 32 users at full 8k. Each step reads 140 GB of weights + 86 GB of KV = 226 GB → 16.9 ms.
  - → ≈ **59 tokens/s per user**, ≈ 1,900 tokens/s in total.
  - One user at 8k: 94 tokens/s. Batch 32 → 20× the throughput, each user 1.6× slower.

sections.title: 6. Batching and KV memory management
sections.body:
- Why batch: one weight read serves the whole batch → cost per token falls.
- Cap: KV memory first (each sequence has its own cache), then compute. → KV size sets how many users one GPU serves.
- **Static batching**: the batch starts and ends together. It waits for the longest sequence; finished slots sit idle.
- **Continuous (in-flight) batching** (Orca): schedule per decode step. A finished sequence leaves at once; a waiting one joins.
- **PagedAttention** (vLLM): KV in fixed-size blocks, like OS memory pages. vLLM's default: 16 tokens per block.
  - Old way: one contiguous slab per sequence, reserved for the maximum length. The vLLM paper measured only 20–38% of KV memory holding real tokens.
  - Paged: waste < 1 block per sequence (16 × 320 KiB = 5 MiB). Shared prefixes can share blocks.
- Example on 4 H100s: 320 GB × 0.9 − 140 GB of weights ≈ 148 GB for KV. Users average 2k tokens; the maximum is 8k.
  - Reserve 8k each (2.5 GiB): ≈ **55** sequences.
  - Paged, pay for 2k each: ≈ **220** sequences.
- Paging does not shrink a token's KV. It stops paying for tokens that never come.

sections.title: 7. Splitting across GPUs, and training memory
sections.body:
- **Tensor parallelism (TP)**: split each layer's matrices across GPUs. Every layer needs all-reduces between them.
  - Needs fast links (NVLink, 900 GB/s on H100). Lowers latency: all GPUs work on every token.
  - Example: TP = 4, each GPU holds 1/4 of every layer.
- **Pipeline parallelism (PP)**: different layers on different GPUs (80 layers / 4 = 20 each).
  - Less communication: only activations pass between stages.
  - Stages wait on each other (bubbles). Raises throughput with many requests in flight, not single-request latency.
- Common layout: TP inside a server (NVLink), PP across servers (slower network).
- **Training memory** with Adam in mixed precision: ≈ **16 bytes per parameter** = bf16 weights 2 + gradients 2 + fp32 master weights 4 + Adam moments 8.
  - 70B → ≈ 1.12 TB before activations.
  - ZeRO/FSDP shard these states across GPUs: 64 GPUs → ≈ 17.5 GB each.

sections.title: 8. Speedups: what changes the output and what does not
sections.body:
- **Prompt caching**: keep the KV cache of a repeated prompt prefix; the next request skips that prefill.
  - Example: every request starts with the same 6,000-token system prompt (≈ 1.8 GiB of KV). Cached → no 0.2 s prefill for it; faster time to first token, cheaper.
  - Needs a **byte-identical prefix**. A timestamp at the start of the prompt makes every prefix new.
  - Output: unchanged.
- **Speculative decoding**: a small draft model proposes $k$ tokens; the big model checks all $k$ in one pass.
  - That pass costs about as much as one token: decode is bandwidth-bound, so the weights are read once.
  - Rejection sampling keeps the big model's output distribution **exactly**.
  - Tokens per big-model pass (Leviathan eq. 1), acceptance rate $\alpha$:
$$\mathbb{E}[\text{tokens}] = \frac{1 - \alpha^{k+1}}{1 - \alpha}$$
  - Example: $\alpha = 0.8$, $k = 4$ → $(1 - 0.8^5)/0.2 \approx 3.36$ tokens per pass, minus the draft model's cost.
- **Quantization**: fewer bytes to read → faster decode and more room for KV. Output: changes a little.

sections.title: 9. Where I get confused
sections.body:
- The KV cache avoids recomputing the past; it does not avoid reading it. Each step still attends to every cached token.
- KV per token uses the **KV heads** ($h_{kv} = 8$), not the query heads (64).
- Forgetting the 2 (K and V) halves the cache estimate.
- Sizing only the weights. 32 users at 8k add 86 GB, more than one H100.
- MoE: memory follows **total** parameters, compute follows **active**.
- Decode is bandwidth-bound: more FLOPS do not help one sequence. Fewer bytes (quantization) do.
- The roofline batch (≈ 300) is for **weights**. KV reads grow with the batch and stay bandwidth-bound.
- PagedAttention removes waste. It does not shrink a token's KV; fp8 KV or fewer KV heads do.
- Static batching waits for the longest sequence; continuous batching refills every step.
- TP lowers latency but needs NVLink; PP tolerates slow links but adds bubbles.
- Speculative decoding and prompt caching keep the output. Quantization does not, quite.

llm-05-inference.summary:
### Phases
- Prefill: whole prompt, parallel, compute-bound → time to first token.
- Decode: one token per step, bandwidth-bound → time per token.
- KV cache works because of the causal mask.
### Memory
- Weights = params × bytes (2 · 1 · 0.5). 70B bf16 = 140 GB.
- KV/token = $2 L h_{kv} d_{head} b$. 70B: 320 KiB; 8k → 2.5 GiB; 32 users → 86 GB.
- Serve 70B, 32 × 8k: ≈ 250 GB → 4 × H100.
- MoE: memory = total, compute = active.
- Train with Adam: 16 B/param.
### Speed
- Decode ceiling ≈ bandwidth / bytes read per step.
- Roofline: H100 ≈ 295 FLOPs/byte → weights stop binding near batch 300.
- KV reads grow with batch.
### Serving
- Continuous batching: refill every step. Paged KV: no reserved waste.
- TP: inside a node, lower latency. PP: across nodes, bubbles.
### Speedups
- Prompt cache: identical prefix, skips prefill.
- Speculative: $(1-\alpha^{k+1})/(1-\alpha)$ tokens per pass, exact output.
- Quantize: faster and smaller, output shifts a little.

questions.stem: Why can a decoder-only LLM cache the K and V of past tokens and reuse them at every step?

options.t: The causal mask: a token's K and V depend only on itself and earlier tokens, so new tokens never change them
options.why: Compute once, store, reuse.

options.t: The weights are frozen at inference
options.why: Not enough: in a bidirectional encoder the weights are frozen too, but a new token changes every old token's vectors.

options.t: K and V are the same in every layer
options.why: Each layer has its own K and V; that is why the cache size has the factor $L$.

options.t: Attention only looks at the last token
options.why: The new token attends to every cached token. The cache avoids recomputing them, not reading them.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between prefill and decode, what limits each, and which user-facing latency each sets.
questions.answer: Prefill runs the whole prompt in one parallel pass and fills the KV cache; it does many FLOPs per weight read, so it is compute-bound, and it sets the time to first token. Decode generates one token per step; each step reads all the weights and the KV cache for little compute, so it is memory-bandwidth-bound, and it sets the time per output token.

questions.stem: Llama-3-70B shape: 80 layers, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, bf16. KV cache per token?

options.t: 320 KiB
options.why: $2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 327{,}680$ bytes.

options.t: 160 KiB
options.why: That forgets the 2 for K and V.

options.t: 2.5 MiB
options.why: That uses the 64 query heads. With GQA only the 8 KV heads are cached.

options.t: 640 KiB
options.why: That uses 4 bytes per value (fp32). bf16 is 2.

questions.stem: Serve the 70B model in bf16 to 32 concurrent users at 8k context (KV 320 KiB per token) on H100 80 GB. Minimum sensible number of GPUs?

options.t: 4: weights 140 GB + KV ≈ 86 GB + overhead ≈ 250–270 GB
options.why: 4 × 80 = 320 GB fits with room; the 64 heads split evenly over 4 GPUs.

options.t: 2: the weights are 140 GB
options.why: That sizes only the weights. The 32 caches add ≈ 86 GB.

options.t: 3: 226 GB fits in 240 GB
options.why: No room for activations and fragmentation, and 64 heads do not split evenly over 3 GPUs.

options.t: 8: one GPU per 4 users
options.why: Works, but double what the memory needs.

questions.stem: The 70B service runs out of memory at 32 users × 8k, and you cannot add GPUs. Which change does **not** reduce the KV bytes each token needs?

options.t: Switching to paged KV allocation (PagedAttention)
options.why: Paging removes reserved but unused memory. A stored token still takes 320 KiB.

options.t: Storing the KV cache in fp8
options.why: 1 byte instead of 2: halves each token's KV.

options.t: A model with fewer KV heads (GQA/MQA)
options.why: $h_{kv}$ is a factor in the per-token formula.

options.t: Sliding-window attention
options.why: It caps how many past tokens each sequence keeps.

questions.stem: The 70B model in bf16 runs on 4 H100s (3.35 TB/s each) with tensor parallelism. One user, short context. Upper bound on decode speed?

options.t: About 96 tokens/s
options.why: Each step reads 140 GB of weights; together the GPUs read 13.4 TB/s → 13.4 / 0.14 ≈ 96.

options.t: About 24 tokens/s
options.why: That uses one GPU's bandwidth. With TP each GPU reads only its quarter of the weights.

options.t: About 28,000 tokens/s
options.why: That is the compute bound ($4 \times 989$ TFLOPS / $2N$). One sequence cannot use the compute; bandwidth binds first.

options.t: About 383 tokens/s
options.why: That is with int4 weights (35 GB).

questions.stem: H100: 989 TFLOPS dense bf16, 3.35 TB/s. Decoding with bf16 weights, at about what batch size do weight reads stop being the bottleneck?

options.t: About 300
options.why: Each 2-byte weight gives 2 FLOPs per sequence: 1 FLOP/byte. The GPU balances at 989/3.35 ≈ 295 FLOPs/byte.

options.t: About 600
options.why: That counts 1 FLOP per 2-byte weight. A multiply-add is 2 FLOPs: 1 FLOP per byte.

options.t: 1: decode is always compute-bound
options.why: At batch 1, decode does 1 FLOP per byte read, far below 295: bandwidth-bound.

options.t: About 3,000

questions.stem: 4 H100s (13.4 TB/s), 70B in bf16 (140 GB). 32 users, each with 8k tokens of context (86 GB of KV in total). Roughly how fast does each user see tokens?

options.t: About 59 tokens/s (≈ 1,900 tokens/s in total)
options.why: Each step reads weights and every cache: 226 GB / 13.4 TB/s ≈ 16.9 ms.

options.t: About 96 tokens/s (≈ 3,060 in total)
options.why: That ignores the KV reads, which grow with the batch.

options.t: About 3 tokens/s
options.why: That treats the 32 users as served one after another. One weight read serves the whole batch.

options.t: About 156 tokens/s
options.why: That divides by the KV bytes only (86 GB). The weights are read each step too.

questions.stem: 148 GB is left for KV (320 KiB per token). Users average 2k tokens; the maximum is 8k. How many sequences fit with contiguous reservation at the maximum, and with paged KV?

options.t: About 55 and about 220
options.why: Reserved: 148 GB / 2.68 GB per 8k sequence ≈ 55. Paged: pay for 2k → 0.67 GB each ≈ 220.

options.t: About 55 both ways
options.why: Paging allocates blocks as tokens arrive; it does not reserve the maximum.

options.t: About 220 and about 880
options.why: Too high: 2k tokens × 320 KiB ≈ 0.67 GB per sequence.

options.t: About 110 and about 440
options.why: That counts 160 KiB per token, forgetting the 2 for K and V.

questions.stem: A model needs 16 GPUs: two servers with 8 GPUs each. NVLink inside a server, a slower network between them. How do you split it?

options.t: Tensor parallelism inside each server, pipeline parallelism across the two
options.why: TP all-reduces every layer and needs NVLink. PP only passes activations between stages, so the slow link can carry it.

options.t: Tensor parallelism across all 16 GPUs
options.why: Every layer's all-reduce would cross the slow network.

options.t: Pipeline parallelism with 16 stages
options.why: Works, but 16 stages add bubbles and latency, and waste the NVLink inside each server.

options.t: Data parallelism: a full copy of the model on each GPU
options.why: The model needs 16 GPUs of memory; a full copy does not fit on one.

questions.stem: Speculative decoding with $k = 4$ draft tokens and acceptance rate $\alpha = 0.8$. Expected tokens per big-model pass?

options.t: About 3.36
options.why: $(1 - 0.8^{5}) / (1 - 0.8) \approx 3.36$: accepted drafts plus the one token the big model always adds.
That assumes every draft is accepted.
That is $\alpha k$. Acceptance stops at the first rejection, and the big model always adds one token.

options.t: About 1.25
options.why: That is $1/\alpha$, not the expected run length.

questions.stem: Every request starts with the same 6,000-token system prompt, and prompt caching is on, but the time to first token never improves. The prompt begins with `Today is 2026-11-24 09:41:07`. Diagnosis?

options.t: The timestamp changes the prefix on every request, so no cached prefix ever matches
options.why: The cache needs a byte-identical prefix. Move changing content to the end.

options.t: The KV cache is too small for 6,000 tokens
options.why: 6,000 × 320 KiB ≈ 1.8 GiB: small next to the GPU memory.

options.t: Decode is bandwidth-bound
options.why: True, but time to first token is set by prefill, which caching would skip.

options.t: Speculative decoding is off
options.why: Speculative decoding speeds decode, not the prefill before the first token.
